opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, because I've spent most of my career in the U.S., and over the past few years I've been watching what's happening in China very closely.

On the robotics side, what strikes me most about China is the speed and the depth of the hardware ecosystem. If you want to build a robot, you need motors, reducers, sensors, batteries, and structural parts, and in places like Shenzhen, Hangzhou, or the Yangtze River Delta the whole supply chain is within a few hours' drive. A team can design a new actuator, get it machined, test it, and iterate in a week or two. In Silicon Valley the same loop can take months, and it costs a lot more. That's a big reason we've seen so many Chinese humanoid and quadruped companies appear so quickly, and why their hardware costs have come down so dramatically. Cost matters enormously in robotics, because if you want robots to learn from real-world data, you need a lot of robots out there collecting it.

Silicon Valley's strength, I think, is still on the intelligence side: foundation models, large-scale learning, and the willingness to bet on very long-horizon, somewhat crazy ideas. There's a culture of asking, "What if we just scale this up and see what happens?" Researchers are given a lot of freedom and compute to explore directions that might not pay off for five years. A lot of the breakthroughs in robot learning, like sim-to-real, large behavior models, and vision-language-action models, came out of that environment.

On research culture, I'd put it this way. In China there's a very strong execution culture. Once a direction is clear, teams move incredibly fast, work very hard, and are very pragmatic: they want to ship something that works and get it into customers' hands. The downside is that there's sometimes less tolerance for exploring directions that aren't obviously going to work, and there can be a tendency for many teams to converge on the same thing at once. In the Valley there's more emphasis on first-principles thinking and on being the first to define a new problem, but sometimes less urgency about turning research into a real product.

What I find exciting is that the two cultures are increasingly learning from each other. Chinese teams are publishing more original work and open-sourcing strong models, and U.S. teams are realizing that you can't just do robotics in simulation or on paper; you need to build real hardware at scale. I think the field as a whole benefits from that. Robotics is a very hard problem. It needs both the bold research vision and the engineering muscle to make things real, so the healthiest outcome is for both sides to keep pushing and keep exchanging ideas.

r001.rationale: The response says Silicon Valley teams bet on long-horizon ideas and give researchers freedom and compute to explore directions that may not pay off for five years, conveying commitment before results are established.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I get asked a lot, and my honest answer is that the two ecosystems are strong in almost opposite ways, and both have something to learn from the other.

On the hardware side, China is simply ahead right now. If you look at humanoids, quadrupeds, dexterous hands, actuators, the supply chain in Shenzhen and Hangzhou lets a team go from a design to a working prototype in weeks, at a cost that would be unthinkable in the Bay Area. Companies like Unitree can iterate on a new leg or a new motor many times in a year. In Silicon Valley, if you want a custom actuator, you're often waiting months and paying ten times as much. That speed of physical iteration compounds. It's why so many of the robots you see in demo videos, even from American labs, are built on Chinese hardware.

On the software and research side, I'd say Silicon Valley still has an edge, but it's narrower than people think. The big foundation-model efforts, the large-scale data collection, the "let's bet on scaling and see what happens" mentality, that culture came out of places like Google, OpenAI, and the Stanford and Berkeley labs. There's a tolerance for long, uncertain research bets and for publishing negative results that I think is still more mature there.

The research culture difference is the part I find most interesting. In China, the energy is incredible. People work extremely hard, they are very fast at following and improving on a promising direction, and the engineering execution is excellent. When a paper comes out from the US showing a new approach, you'll see three or four very good Chinese reproductions and improvements within months. That's a real strength. The weakness, historically, has been in defining the problem in the first place. Fewer groups were willing to spend three years on something nobody else believed in. But that's changing quickly. The younger generation of PIs who came back from the US or Europe, and increasingly the ones trained entirely in China, are much more willing to set their own agenda rather than chase the leaderboard.

The other thing I'd point out is talent flow. A huge fraction of the robotics researchers in Silicon Valley are Chinese or Chinese-trained. So in some sense it's not two separate cultures, it's one community with two centers of gravity, and ideas move back and forth constantly. The geopolitical friction is making that harder, and I think that hurts both sides.

If I had to summarize: China has the bodies, Silicon Valley has the brains, and the race over the next few years is really about who can close their gap faster. My guess is China closes the software gap faster than the US closes the hardware gap, because algorithms travel more easily than supply chains. But the groups that will really win are the ones that can combine both, and I'm seeing more of those on both sides of the Pacific.

r001.rationale: The response says Silicon Valley tolerates “long, uncertain research bets,” including a willingness to bet on scaling and see what happens. This conveys committing to ideas before their results are certain.

astra-6.text:
I think China has tremendous strengths in robotics, especially in manufacturing and the ability to turn an idea into a physical product quickly. When you build robots, access to components, suppliers, and people who understand manufacturing makes a huge difference. You need to test something, see what breaks, and build the next version.

Silicon Valley has a different set of strengths. There’s a culture of bringing together people from different disciplines, questioning assumptions, and pursuing ideas whose commercial value may not be obvious yet. That can be very productive for research, although the pressure to show results exists in both places.

I’d be careful about drawing too sharp a distinction, though. There are teams in China doing very ambitious, long-term research, and teams in Silicon Valley focused on near-term products. For me, the important question is how you connect those two modes: give researchers enough freedom to explore, while making sure their ideas eventually work on a real robot in a real environment. Robotics needs both.

r001.rationale: The response says Silicon Valley teams pursue ideas whose commercial value may not be obvious, but it does not communicate a willingness to commit resources before those ideas produce initial results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think China has some real advantages in robotics, especially when it comes to turning an idea into a physical system. There’s a strong manufacturing ecosystem, a lot of engineering talent, and people are willing to move quickly. In robotics, that matters because progress often comes from building something, testing it, seeing what breaks, and trying again.

Silicon Valley also moves quickly, but its research culture tends to give people more room to pursue uncertain ideas and challenge existing approaches. Universities, startups, and research labs exchange ideas and talent, and that can help a promising research direction become a new company.

Of course, there’s a lot of variation within both places. I wouldn’t say one culture is simply better. The opportunity is to combine strong execution with the freedom to take research risks. For robotics, we need both: ambitious ideas and the patience to make them work reliably in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says Silicon Valley allows room for uncertain ideas, but does not describe committing resources to ideas before they produce initial results.
